transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-07
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 60 mins
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Marcus Ng (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (CTO - CareSync), Sofia Ramirez (Security Architect), Daniel Cho (Platform Eng), Priya Patel (Compliance)

Summary: Quick scope session to align POC goals: private networking options, data residency (US/EU), egress/egress-limited environments, and perf benchmarks. Agree on deliverables and schedule pilot kickoff.

00:00 Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, quick introductions please
00:08 Alex Morgan: yeah, alex here, cto at caresync, thanks for setting up, our main ask is we need to validate private connectivity and that data never leaves our org's region, and also performance numbers for our expected workload
00:20 Jordan Lee: great, the Redwood team today is me, priya se, and marcus, we'll focus on the se-level details. quick confirm, is this a cloud-only pilot or do you have on-prem workloads?
00:35 Daniel Cho: primarily cloud, aws first, we want us-east-1 and potentially eu-west-1 for our eu patients, and in some cases we have restricted egress from certain subnets, so any egress to public internet is sensitive
00:50 Priya Kapoor: ok, and from an infra standpoint, are you leaning toward VPC peering or PrivateLink/Interface endpoints? both have tradeoffs we should call out
01:02 Sofia Ramirez: security's leaning to PrivateLink because peering requires broad CIDR permissions and we like more control, but cost and throughput are concerns, so that's why we wanted the POC
01:15 Marcus Ng: quick note, Redwood's private option offers a customer-managed VPC peering or PrivateLink style connection to the dedicated serving fleet. There is also a private control plane option for enterprise where control plane comms can be in a customer VPC. We'll send details in the guide
01:30 Alex Morgan: ok, success criteria for us: 1) data never leaves selected regions (us-east-1 or eu-west-1), 2) 95th percentile latency for 512-token responses under 150ms, 3) ability to sustain 50 concurrent requests with burst to 100, 4) logs and audit trail stored in our S3 with KMS encryption. POC should show baseline throughput and also failover behaviour
02:05 Priya Kapoor: sounds reasonable. couple clarifying q's: when you say 512-token responses, do you mean generation length or input+output?
02:12 Alex Morgan: good point, let's set generation output avg ~256 tokens, context up to 512, but benchmark will exercise up to 1k tokens end-to-end. We can provide sample prompts
02:27 Jordan Lee: noted. for the 50 concurrent requests, is that steady-state or peak?
02:33 Daniel Cho: steady-state target is 50, peaks of 100 for short periods, also cost sensitivity — we want to see dedicated throughput vs hosted pricing implications
02:47 Marcus Ng: for connectivity: VPC peering gives lower latency and no data-path hops but requires cross-account peering and careful CIDR planning; it can be simpler but it's not transitive. PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink) uses interface endpoints and scales well per NLB and is more controlled from a security standpoint, but you pay for ENIs and data processing, and egress path is through the endpoint service. Also PrivateLink works better for multi-account isolation
03:12 Sofia Ramirez: and does Redwood support both in the private offering?
03:16 Priya Kapoor: yes, we support both. For the POC we typically test PrivateLink first if security requires it, and run a small peering test if latency targets are tight. We'll provide a checklist for both and required IAM/account info
03:31 Alex Morgan: region/failover question: can we keep EU data in eu-west-1 and not replicate to us-east-1? we need residency and policy controls
03:40 Jordan Lee: yes, customers can choose region mappings and model hosting, we can host the POC in eu-west-1 for EU tests and in us-east-1 for US tests. we'll document storage location for logs and artifacts — if you want logs pushed to your S3 in eu-west-1 that's supported
03:52 Sofia Ramirez: what about KMS? we need to use our CMKs, HSM style is ideal
03:56 Marcus Ng: we integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest, and for private deployments we support customer-managed CMKs. we'll add the KMS config instructions to the security doc
04:10 Priya Kapoor: on benchmarks — we propose two tracks: functional correctness (latency and token p95/p99 for a set of prompts) and throughput (concurrent requests, sustained tokens/day). For the POC we recommend: 1) baseline with 1 client at different seq lengths, 2) ramp to 50 concurrency, 3) burst test to 100, 4) steady state 24h run to estimate tokens/day and cache hit rates
04:40 Daniel Cho: can you share the scripts? we prefer something we can run from our CICD to replicate tests
04:45 Priya Kapoor: yes, we'll share a JMeter/postman/golang script set that hits the endpoints via the private link, and a small perf harness to parse p95/p99
04:53 Alex Morgan: do we need to open ports or specific SG rules?
04:56 Marcus Ng: for PrivateLink you'll create interface endpoints in your VPC and we'll provide the service name to connect. SGs typically allow HTTPS outbound to the endpoint's ENIs; for peering you'll update route tables. We'll include exact SG/route examples in the doc
05:10 Sofia Ramirez: egress constraints — some of our subnets are egress-blocked to public internet. can the POC work entirely inside those subnets?
05:18 Priya Kapoor: yes, if you use PrivateLink the traffic stays private. if you have egress-blocked subnets we just need the endpoint ENIs to be routable. For peering you'd need route access but no internet egress if the destination is the peered VPC
05:35 Alex Morgan: what about billing and egress charges? we need to model cost impact for data processing and inter-AZ charges
05:42 Marcus Ng: PrivateLink has per-GB data processing fees plus endpoint hours; peering has inter-region transfer costs if cross-region, and aws data transfer within same region is often free or minimal but depends on AZs. we'll provide an example cost calc using your expected tokens/day
06:00 Jordan Lee: timeline: propose 2-week POC: week 1 - network setup and baseline small benchmarks; week 2 - scale tests and security validations. Kickoff target week of 2025-05-19. deliverables: benchmark report, network runbook, security checklist, and a follow-up review
06:20 Daniel Cho: dev ops note, we'll need Redwood's account ids and service names to set up endpoints, we'll also share our CIDR ranges and three test subnets
06:30 Alex Morgan: ok we'll collect that by 2025-05-12, plus our compliance team will review the security whitepaper
06:40 Priya Patel: on compliance, we require SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 evidence plus a list of data flows for audit, also want retention policy discussion
06:50 Marcus Ng: we'll attach SOC2 summary, ISO cert references, and a dataflow template, and note retention controls and logs export options to your S3 with CMK encryption
07:05 Priya Kapoor: any performance targets beyond p95 latency <150ms? p99 for 1k tokens might be higher but we will capture both; also want to measure cold-start latency for model variants
07:20 Alex Morgan: yes capture p50/p95/p99 and cold-start numbers, and also error rates under load, and throttling behavior
07:30 Jordan Lee: quick note: for model selection, do you need a specific model family? open models or Redwood curated models?
07:36 Daniel Cho: we want an LLM comparable to gpt-3.5 quality for now, but cost conscious; we'll try a 13B quantized variant first and maybe test a 33B if performance allows
07:50 Priya Kapoor: ok we'll propose a quantized 13B in the POC and a 33B baseline run for throughput comparison, and include model config in the benchmark doc
08:05 Alex Morgan: what about fallback — if private capacity is constrained, can we failover to hosted with no data crossing our reserved VPC?
08:15 Marcus Ng: failover to hosted is possible but you'd need to accept egress to Redwood's hosted cluster; for strict residency you'd prefer a dedicated fallback in the same region. We can discuss hybrid fallback policies in the runbook
08:30 Sofia Ramirez: for audit, we need request-level logs and KMS-wrapped keys, plus RBAC for who can trigger rollout changes
08:42 Jordan Lee: Redwood Console supports token-level tracing and RBAC. We'll surface audit logs to your S3 and provide per-route dashboards. We'll note access controls in the security doc
08:55 Alex Morgan: great. to recap, deliverables: network guide (peering/privatelink steps), security whitepaper + SOC2 artifacts, perf harness and scripts, initial benchmark run results, and cost estimate. POC kickoff w/c 2025-05-19 pending CIDRs and account ids
09:20 Jordan Lee: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and the docs. any last q's?
09:26 Sofia Ramirez: none from security, thanks
09:28 Daniel Cho: we'll coordinate internal calendar invites for kickoff
09:30 Jordan Lee: awesome, we'll follow up with next steps and action items

Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors present; names sometimes mis-attributed. This transcript is verbatim-ish and contains filler and interruptions.
